skill.name: Features that fit the purpose (tense, headings, command verbs)
skill.why: The right features help a text do its job, and help you read it.
skill.how: Ask what the text is for. Then check its tense, headings and verbs fit.

beats.say: Each kind of text has its own tools.
Instructions start with a bossy word that says what to do.
That bossy word is called a command verb.
Recounts already happened, so they use past tense.

beats.say: Reports use headings, so readers can find facts fast.
beats.show: **Food**: Possums eat seeds, berries and moths.

encounters.frame: The Fittlet is helping Wren finish her report on blue whales for the Scaffold Peaks library.
encounters.text: Blue Whales. Blue whales live in every ocean in the world, from the icy waters near Antarctica to warm seas near the equator. An adult blue whale can grow to about thirty metres long, which is longer than two buses parked end to end. Its heart is about the size of a small car, and it beats only a few times a minute when the whale dives. Despite their huge size, blue whales eat some of the smallest animals in the sea. They gulp enormous mouthfuls of water, then push it out through bristly plates called baleen, which trap tiny shrimp called krill. A single blue whale can eat around four tonnes of krill in one day. Their skin is blue-grey with pale spots, but it looks bright blue underwater. Blue whales make deep, rumbling calls that can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater. Scientists think they use these calls to find each other across the empty ocean. Blue whales can live for eighty or ninety years.

encounters.text: Wedge-tailed Eagles. Wedge-tailed eagles are the largest birds of prey in Australia, with wings that can stretch more than two metres from tip to tip. They are found all over the mainland and in Tasmania, from deserts and farmland to the high, snowy country around Scaffold Peaks. Adults are mostly dark brown, almost black, while young birds are a lighter, golden brown that darkens as they age. The eagle gets its name from its long tail, which is shaped like a wedge and helps it steer as it soars on warm, rising air. Like other birds of prey, they have hooked beaks for tearing meat and strong, curved claws called talons for gripping. Wedge-tailed eagles hunt rabbits, lizards and other small animals, and they also feed on animals that are already dead. Their eyesight is so sharp that they can spot a rabbit moving from more than a kilometre away. They can soar higher than almost any other Australian bird, sometimes more than a kilometre above the ground. Pairs often stay together for many years and return to the same nesting area each spring. A pair usually raises one or two chicks a year, and both parents take turns bringing food to the nest.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing a report called 'The Human Nose'. The Fittlet swallowed one of his sub-headings.
encounters.text: ___ Snot might be revolting, but your body would be in serious trouble without it. Its first job is to trap things. Every time you breathe in, the sticky snot lining your nose catches dust, pollen and germs before they can reach your lungs. Its second job is to keep the inside of your nose moist, because a dry nose cracks and bleeds easily. Some snot even traps specks of smoke and tiny bugs, holding them until they can be swept away. Snot also warms and dampens the air on its way in, so that cold, dry air doesn't irritate your lungs. It even contains special chemicals that attack some germs, which means it works a little like a security guard at the door. Without snot, every breath would carry dirt and germs straight into your chest. Tiny hairs called cilia sweep the dirty snot towards the back of your throat, where you swallow it without noticing, dust and all. When you catch a cold, your nose makes extra snot to flush the germs out, which is why it runs. Your nose makes fresh snot all day long, so this protection never runs out. So the next time you need a tissue, remember that your snot is busy keeping you healthy.

encounters.success: Every sentence is about what snot does for your body: trapping, wetting, warming and fighting germs.

encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the text it fits.
encounters.success: The procedure uses command verbs: check, leave, head. The explanation uses present tense to show how tides always work.

items.text: Check the tide chart at the beach hut before you walk out to the rock pools.
items.reason: 'Check' is a command verb. It tells the reader what to do.

items.text: Because the Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean, the water bulges out towards it.
items.reason: This gives a cause, in present tense. It explains how tides work.

items.text: As Earth spins, each beach passes through a bulge, and the tide comes in.
items.reason: This explains what makes the tide come in, in present tense.

items.text: Leave yourself at least an hour to get back before the water returns.
items.reason: 'Leave' is a command verb. It tells the reader what to do.

items.text: When the beach moves away from the bulge, the water drains back and the tide goes out.
items.reason: This explains what makes the tide go out. It doesn't tell anyone to do anything.

items.text: Once the tide has turned, head straight back to the sand without stopping.
items.reason: It starts with when, but 'head' is a command verb. It tells the reader what to do.

items.text: Earth spins once a day and the Moon pulls up a bulge on each side, so most beaches get two high tides daily.
